clinicalPearls: Classically presents in the first months of life with irritability, fever and tender soft-tissue swelling overlying affected bones
The mandible is the most frequently involved bone, followed by the clavicle, ribs and long bones, producing subperiosteal cortical hyperostosis on radiographs
The familial autosomal dominant form is caused by a recurrent heterozygous variant in COL1A1 affecting type I collagen
Soft-tissue swelling is characteristically firm and non-pitting and overlies the hyperostotic bone rather than a joint
The condition is self-limiting, with hyperostosis typically regressing over weeks to months and remodelling leaving little or no long-term deformity
Inflammatory markers may be raised during acute episodes, which can mimic infection or non-accidental injury and cause diagnostic confusion
Management is supportive, with analgesia and reassurance; the disorder resolves without the need for surgery in the great majority of cases
reference.pathophysiology: The familial form of Caffey disease is caused by a recurrent heterozygous missense variant in COL1A1, which encodes the alpha-1 chain of type I collagen. The altered collagen is thought to provoke an inflammatory, periosteal reaction with exuberant subperiosteal new bone formation over affected cortices, accompanied by overlying soft-tissue swelling. The process is dynamic and self-resolving: the acute hyperostotic phase gives way to gradual resorption and remodelling as the child grows. The predilection for the mandible, clavicle and diaphyses of tubular bones, together with fever and raised inflammatory markers, reflects this transient inflammatory bone response rather than a persistent dysplasia.
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs demonstrating subperiosteal cortical hyperostosis, especially of the mandible and clavicle
Inflammatory markers to characterise the acute episode and help distinguish from infection
Full blood count and other tests to exclude sepsis or malignancy where clinically indicated
Skeletal survey to define the distribution and exclude features of non-accidental injury
COL1A1 molecular genetic testing in familial or recurrent cases
Serial imaging to confirm the expected spontaneous regression
redFlags: Persistent or progressive swelling and hyperostosis beyond the expected self-limiting course, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
Features suggesting osteomyelitis such as localised warmth, systemic toxicity or a discharging sinus
Radiographic or clinical findings raising concern for non-accidental injury
Involvement pattern or systemic illness suggesting malignancy such as metastatic neuroblastoma
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent, with spontaneous resolution of the hyperostosis and soft-tissue swelling over weeks to months and generally complete bony remodelling, although occasional cases have recurrent episodes or residual deformity.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the tender swelling and raised inflammatory markers as osteomyelitis and administering unnecessary prolonged antibiotics
Wrongly attributing the periosteal changes to non-accidental injury, with serious consequences for the family
Overlooking the mandibular predilection, which is a strong diagnostic clue
Intervening surgically for a condition that characteristically resolves on its own
references: Resnick's Diagnosis of Bone and Joint Disorders
management: Manage acute episodes supportively with simple analgesia and anti-inflammatory medication for the pain and irritability.
Reassure families that the hyperostosis is self-limiting and typically regresses over weeks to months.
Confirm the expected spontaneous regression and remodelling with serial radiographs, avoiding unnecessary intervention.
Exclude mimics such as infection, malignancy and non-accidental injury before settling on the diagnosis.
Offer COL1A1 molecular testing and genetic counselling for the autosomal dominant familial form.
Follow up for the uncommon recurrence or residual deformity.
